LegoZendo.note: v3 run1: crack r3 (kid-proxy, diagnostic grids per clue letter) + crack r6 (experimentalist, by recolouring/cropping/concatenating demo walls). LEAK: count is additive over separated regions and invariant under relabelling, so demos are reusable answers. Possible fixes (owner's call): forbid unconnected layouts again, or pin one brick position from the clue, or require the clue letter's brick count to equal a clue-derived number.

qual.advice: Shrink the grid (keep demos in the ~12x32 regime, cap y lower) so a kid can see a whole layout and tell a 1-pin touch from 2- or 3-pin by eye within 20 minutes.
Cut the background filler so the mosaic reads as Lego instantly; the width-2 two-colour join count reads to an LLM as bipartite edge counting.

Wordz.note: run1: both cracked (r3, r4). Alternation found via near-miss pairs / control rows; hidden dictionary discovered from false positives. Too easy for Opus.

qual.advice: Anchor in a drawable object; alternating vowel/consonant counting is a well-known word-puzzle genre an LLM guesses by pattern.
The double-nibble clause is positive-only and easy to miss; consider widening the fish-minus-leaf gap to 2+ in every demo so the nose/tail-vs-both-sides distinction reads as the headline discovery.

The nose-vs-tail insight is a great kid-native discovery, but the wide multi-row grid with strict exact-width lines and many decoy fish makes the format a slog; shrinking the grid or cleaning alignment would free more of the kid's 20 minutes for the insight.

tovel.note: run1: both partial (48%, 83%) without the rule. LEAK: accepted shapes are invariant under letter renaming and depend only on (days,start,N) -> 140 triples farmable via demos+probes. Refiner lever: tie the count to letter identity (a second clue letter, or a required count of the clue letter) so shapes don't transfer.

qual.advice: Place the weekend-reaching and week-break-crossing decoy pairs near a counted pair in every demo so the school-week exclusion is spottable by contrast.

The k-count of two-apart same-letter pairs is easy to spot from the demos, but nothing visually flags that the earliest counted pair must land on day n; consider making the first counted day visually distinct.

Bundling exact count and exact first date onto the skip-day/weekday clause is a lot of simultaneous bookkeeping for 20 minutes; the gap-day-is-different hook risks being buried under position matching.
Four stacked clauses stay un-sayable in one sentence; merge or drop one (fold the blocked middle into the weekday window, or drop first-occurrence=n).

versions.note: v2: clue adds first-counted-day n; closes rename/(days,start,k) farming (100%->11%); decoy pairs in every demo
v3: pair counts only if the day between is not the letter (kills stripe 88%->0%); n placed late; every demo has a blocked xxx run
v4: k 1..5 gives the minimal probe a 22% foothold; uniform header; n later for k>=2

opus-default.priming: Play as a careful experimentalist: harvest clues, then design each round as a controlled experiment cycling candidate answers by memory['_index'].

opus-kidproxy.priming: You are paired with a curious 12-year-old who has never coded. After each demo, narrate the picture to them in plain words, write down the three things a kid would notice first, and let those naive readings drive your first hypotheses. Test the kid's ideas before your own.

opus-lowdemo.constraints: CONSTRAINT: you may request at most 2 demos in the whole game; every other window's demo must go unused.

opus-theorist.priming: Before any probing, spend your first window writing ten hypotheses from the demo alone, phrased as you would explain them to a 12-year-old; then probe only to discriminate between them. Prefer everyday, physical readings of a picture over mathematical ones.

sonnet-default.priming: Play as a careful experimentalist: harvest clues, then design each round as a controlled experiment cycling candidate answers by memory['_index'].

sonnet-kidproxy.priming: You are paired with a curious 12-year-old who has never coded. After each demo, narrate the picture to them in plain words, write down the three things a kid would notice first, and let those naive readings drive your first hypotheses.
